catalog_locator: Phonology section, last prose paragraph (immediately before the Vowels table in the 2026-09-17 rendering). Files re-: (rev 334893559, last paragraph of ==Phonology==) and (wgRevisionId 1341416286).
catalog_quote: Vowels are distinguished for length, with long vowels (aa, ee, etc.) often occurring where a consonant has historically been lost. Vowels can occur alone or in various combinations. Stress is normally on the penultimate syllable of a word. However, syllables that end with a consonant or a long vowel take stress in precedence to other syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress, overridden by heavy syllables: a closed (consonant-final) syllable or a long-vowel syllable attracts stress in preference to a light penult. No statement about which heavy syllable wins when there are several, or about final closed syllables specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the weight override itself; the same section notes that Sa comprises several divergent dialects (western, eastern, northern 'F', southern 'Ha') without saying whether the stress rule differs among them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('syllable of a word'); no discussion of phrase-level stress or citation forms. Same wording pattern as the Apma statement in our earlier reading (weight-hedged), suggesting the same author's field-based generalisation.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement concerns Sa as a whole (saaa1241, ISO sax), with the author noting four divergent dialects (western 'Saa', eastern 'Sa', northern 'F' dialect, southern 'Ha'); no dialect is specified for the stress rule. Gray's website and the Wikipedia examples use the Panngi (western) dialect. The ELAR 'Ha' deposit is mislabelled ISO haq (Ha of Tanzania) and is in fact the southern dialect of Sa. Glottolog lists the Wikipedia dialect names Ponorwal, Lolatavola, Ninebulo; Tryon 1972 gives Ponorwol as an alternate language name.
